title: Government Structure
description: Understand the structure of Nepal's government including the executive, legislative, and judicial branches.

sections.title: Three Branches of Government
sections.content: Nepal follows the principle of separation of powers with three distinct branches: Executive, Legislative, and Judicial. Each branch has specific powers and responsibilities, providing checks and balances to prevent abuse of power. This system ensures democratic governance and protection of citizens' rights.
keyPoints: Executive branch implements and enforces laws
Judicial branch interprets laws and ensures justice
Separation of powers prevents concentration of authority

sections.title: Executive Branch
sections.content: The executive branch is headed by the President as the Head of State and the Prime Minister as the Head of Government. The President performs ceremonial functions and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Prime Minister leads the government and is responsible to the federal parliament. The Council of Ministers assists in policy implementation and administration.
keyPoints: President is the Head of State
Prime Minister is the Head of Government
Council of Ministers assists in governance

sections.title: Legislative Branch - Federal Parliament
sections.content: Nepal has a bicameral federal parliament consisting of the House of Representatives (Lower House) and the National Assembly (Upper House). The House of Representatives has 275 members elected through mixed electoral system. The National Assembly has 59 members representing provinces and special groups. Parliament makes laws, controls public finances, and oversees the executive.
keyPoints: Makes laws and controls public finances

sections.title: Judicial Branch
sections.content: The judicial system is headed by the Supreme Court, followed by High Courts at the provincial level, and District Courts at the local level. The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court, which is the highest court for constitutional interpretation and final appeals. The judiciary is independent and ensures rule of law, constitutional compliance, and protection of fundamental rights.
keyPoints: Supreme Court is the highest judicial authority
High Courts operate at provincial level
Independent judiciary ensures rule of law

sections.title: Checks and Balances in Practice
sections.content: Oversight tools—legislative questioning, budget control, judicial review, and constitutional bodies—form a network restraining concentration of power. Each branch both limits and depends on the others, producing dynamic accountability rather than rigid separation.

sections.title: Inter-Branch Coordination
sections.content: Complex policies (public health, disaster response) require coordinated action—executive implementation, legislative authorization, and judicial assurance of rights compliance. Informal consultation and joint committees can mitigate fragmentation.

sections.title: Accountability Mechanisms
sections.content: Transparency reports, audits, asset declarations, and public hearings reinforce institutional trust. Whistleblower protections and media freedom amplify external checks on misconduct.
keyPoints: Media and civil society extend oversight

sections.title: Comparative Insight
sections.content: Nepal's evolving federal-parliamentary system blends elements from regional parliamentary traditions with localized autonomy commitments. Comparative observation highlights the importance of institutional maturation and adaptive procedural refinement.

sections.title: Historical Institutional Context
sections.content: Institutional arrangements emerged from constitutional negotiations balancing central stability with demands for regional inclusion. Earlier centralized paradigms ceded to layered oversight structures and expanded parliamentary committees.
keyPoints: Negotiated balance of central & regional needs
Shift from centralization to layered governance

sections.title: Practical Governance Interfaces
sections.content: Policy lifecycles span executive drafting, legislative scrutiny, judicial conformity review, and oversight feedback loops. Informal coordination forums supplement formal instruments to expedite multi‑sector initiatives (e.g., disaster response).

sections.title: Emerging Challenges
sections.content: Complex policy domains (climate adaptation, digital regulation) strain existing capacity. Data interoperability, legislative backlog management, and skills development are pivotal for adaptive governance resilience.
keyPoints: Skill development for emerging policy areas

sections.title: Future Outlook
sections.content: Priorities: enhancing evidence use in legislation, digitizing committee workflows, strengthening constitutional body coordination, and embedding civic participation technologies into decision processes.

sections.title: Case Study: Applying Concepts
sections.content: A practical scenario demonstrates how principles from "Government Structure" operate in real life. Consider a local authority decision challenged for compliance with constitutional norms. Analyze actors involved, legal basis, and remedy pathways to understand implementation dynamics.
keyPoints: Reflect on lessons for future decisions

sections.title: Implementation Gaps and Challenges
sections.content: Even with strong legal and policy frameworks, realizing "Government Structure" can face capacity, coordination, and resource constraints. Data quality and awareness gaps may slow progress and produce uneven outcomes across regions.

sections.content: This section clarifies important terms frequently used in "Government Structure" to make core ideas easier to remember and apply.
